news.title: Trump, Hegseth clashed at Camp David as US President felt 'misled' about weapons shortage - report
news.text: US President Donald Trump didn't know about the extreme munitions shortage that is threatening to limit US military options in Iran, the Washington Post reported on Wednesday, citing a source.According to the source, Trump confronted US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David on Friday, saying that he thought the munitions issue "had been fixed," and that he felt he had been misled, the report added.This missile shortage may have been part of the reason that Trump decided not to launch what he described as "the biggest attack since World War II," on Iran over the weekend, the report cited the source as saying.The US Army has used up "virtually all" of its stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles during its five-month war with Iran, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday.These long-range munitions allow the military to carry out accurate strikes from a safe distance, playing a crucial role in the US-Iran conflict.Ukraine feels interceptor shortage after US rejected licenseThe Washington Post found that in the first month of the conflict with Iran, the US had fired more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and over 1,000 Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAD) missiles, and used at least 1,300 tactical ballistic missiles.When asked for comment on the stockpile data, the White House issued a statement from Trump, saying the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world" and "far more than we need," Reuters reported."Our defense companies are, at this moment, making more munitions than they have ever made before, in addition to expanding their plants and equipment at record levels," Trump said.The munitions shortage has an impact beyond the US-Iran conflict. The Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMs) stockpile, a short-range missile also in demand by Ukraine, is drained to the extent that there's basically none left, Reuters reported.Additionally, between February and July the US had used around 65% of its Patriot interceptors, leaving the country unwilling to supply Ukraine with the much needed defense system.At times, the interceptor shortage caused by US use of munitions during the Iran conflict has been deadly in Ukraine.Although in early July President Trump had offered to give Ukraine the license to make Patriot interceptors, last week he denied the claim that the US had agreed to "give away" the technology.On Wednesday, following a deadly Russian attack on Kyiv, Ukrainian President Voldymr Zelenskyy said that the shortage of interceptor missiles "encourages Russia to launch such attacks that take human lives," the BBC reported."Every single day," Zelenskyy said, "the lives of people here in Ukraine depend on the decisiveness of our partners in Europe and America."

news.title: Ohio Rep. Miller rejects calls to leave reelection race as domestic abuse claims surface
news.text: Ohio congressman Max Miller will run for reelection in November despite facing domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, the representative told CNN in an interview on Tuesday.In past months, Miller has faced scrutiny after claims of domestic abuse made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, surfaced in media reports. In May, Miller sued Moreno for defamation, claiming she made "false, malicious, and defamatory statements" about him.Moreno has accused Miller of holding a gun to her head, as well as fracturing their two-year-old daughter's collarbone. Other reported incidents include one when Miller allegedly threw Moreno against a wall. These allegations appeared in police records reviewed by news agencies.In a post to X/Twitter on Sunday, Miller rejected Moreno's accusations."I have never abused our daughter," he said, framing the allegations as made as part of a battle for custody over their daughter. Additionally, he released a series of documents from his divorce and custody cases, which he said supported his version of events.Miller 'fails to meet' standard for politicians, Moreno's father saysThat same day, Moreno's father, Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno said that the process had been "brutal beyond comprehension" for Moreno, and that "if there's any minimum standard for being a public official... [Miller] fails to meet that [standard].In another post to X on Tuesday, Miller said he would file for an ethics investigation into himself."I have absolutely nothing to hide," he wrote. Later that day, the House Ethics Committee said it had opened an investigation into the allegations. US President Donald Trump called Miller a "good person" when asked about the situation.“I know Max. He's a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I'm going to let the families figure that out,” Trump said. Miller previously worked on Trump's first two election campaigns.Behind the scenes, however, the White House wants Miller to let go of his seat at the end of this term, POLITICO reported citing several anonymous sources.Miller said he would keep his reelection bid going n a Tuesday interview with CNN.“No one has told me to get off the ballot, and that's because they know I can win this seat,” he said. Republican colleagues of his have largely refused to call for his withdrawal, with House Speaker Mike Johnson arguing that the ethics investigation should be completed before any decision is made."We always withhold judgment on this, whether it's Republicans or Democrats,” Johnson told POLITICO.Should he change his mind, Miller would need to withdraw from the race by August 10, per Ohio's election rules.

August 5, 2026




 Kisko Amar-I turns life’s storms into hope with new single ‘Survive the Rain’ 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Reggae singer Kisko Amar-I is encouraging listeners to find strength in adversity with his latest single, Survive the Rain, a roots reggae anthem inspired by resilience, faith and personal growth.

The song was sparked by a conversation with a woman whose words left a lasting impression.

“She told me, ‘I survived the rain and used it to grow’. The moment I heard those words, I knew there was a song in them,” Kisko recalled.

While inspired by her story, the singer said the song also reflects his own journey through financial struggles, personal setbacks and moments that tested his faith.

“I’ve learned that our greatest growth often comes during our hardest seasons. I want people to know that no matter what they’re facing, they can survive the rain.”

Released last Friday, the single is a collaboration between Kisko Amar-I Music and Quality Steel Entertainment, recorded on the Roots Riddim. He is also promoting an updated version of Darkest Cloud, edited to improve its radio appeal while preserving its original message.

Kisko recently completed a week-long promotional tour of Jamaica, where he said the response from the media, DJs and fans exceeded his expectations.

“People genuinely connected with the songs and embraced the message behind them. That encouragement reminded me why I continue making music.”

Born in Steer Town, St Ann, and now based in West Palm Beach, Florida, Kisko has remained committed to uplifting, spiritually conscious reggae.

“My purpose is to use music to elevate people and inspire them to grow,” he said.

Looking ahead, Kisko plans to continue releasing authentic roots reggae while expanding his international touring schedule.

“I’m most proud of my stagecraft and performing with a live band. I want to reach more people with music that inspires and stands the test of time,” he said.

August 5, 2026




 Over River Bridge set to reopen before new school year 







INGSTON, Jamaica — The National Works Agency (NWA) is fast-tracking plans to have the Over River Bridge in St James reopened to the public before the start of the new school year.

The Over River Bridge, a Compact Bailey Bridge, was washed away during Hurricane Melissa, cutting off the Over River community from neighbouring areas, including Hurlock and Sign.

The Sign roadway is a popular route used by residents to access Montego Bay’s city centre. Since the bridge was damaged, residents have had to rely on alternative routes, resulting in longer travel times and increased transportation costs.

READ: Help flows for Over River bridge

Community Relations Officer at the NWA’s Western Region, Janel Ricketts, in a statement on Wednesday, said repair work on the bridge began in February 2026 but was delayed due to logistical challenges.

Despite the setbacks, Ricketts said construction has progressed significantly, with the contractor on track to complete the project by September 2026.

She explained that the bridge has since been relaunched after being removed from the river. Steel components have been repaired, and the structure strengthened to support continued use.

The next phase of work will focus on constructing the bridge’s abutment walls and ramps, the NWA said.

Residents are being reminded not to attempt to cross the unfinished bridge while rehabilitation work continues.

Demolition of giant swing underway 

 Latest News, News 

August 5, 2026




 Montego Bay giant swing demolished over lack of approvals 







ST JAMES, Jamaica — A giant swing attraction erected between Mango Walk and Norwood has been demolished following enforcement action by the St James Municipal Corporation.

The demolition was carried out on Wednesday after the corporation said operators ignored notices to cease construction. According to the corporation, the structure was built without the necessary building and planning approvals.

“The St James Municipal Corporation today took enforcement action against the operators of a giant swing tourist attraction operating in the community of Norwood Pen,” the corporation said in a statement.

Giant swing

“Earlier in the day, a cease notice was served after it was discovered that the structure had been erected without the required building or planning approvals. When the enforcement team returned later in the afternoon, they found that the notices had been removed and the premises locked. In response, the acting superintendent of roads and works mobilised the enforcement team to commence demolition of the unauthorised structure,” it continued.

The corporation reminded members of the public that all developments must comply with the provisions of the Building Act and the Town and Country Planning Act.

“While we regret having to take such measures, they are necessary to protect the safety of both residents and visitors. The removal of official notices and the absence of approvals represent a clear disregard for local authority,” it said.

Richard Vernon look on at giant swing

Officials said obtaining the proper approvals would have ensured the structure met safety standards and addressed requirements such as parking facilities, bathrooms, safety measures, attraction licensing, and insurance.

“The corporation’s decision may be unpopular, but it is necessary. We prefer to face criticism rather than risk the loss of life because we failed to act. The St James Municipal Corporation remains committed to supporting the diversification of attractions, but emphasises that such ventures must be pursued in the right way, with full compliance to the law,” it said.

 International News, Latest News 

August 5, 2026




 FIFA apologise for World Cup privatisation plan 







PARIS, France (AFP)—FIFA’s leadership apologised on Wednesday following the controversy over the plan to open the World Cup to private investment while reaffirming its “full support” for president Gianni Infantino.

In a statement, FIFA’s leadership acknowledged “that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media”.

“Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the FIFA Secretary General and members of the FIFA Management Board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 FIFA Member Associations,” the statement added.

Infantino has come under increasing pressure, even from within his organisation, over his handling of the proposal, and calls for him to step down have grown since he abandoned it last Saturday.

FIFA floated the plan, saying it could raise up to $4.2 billion based on a valuation of $20 billion for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

It said that, if approved, the project could provide each of FIFA’s 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027, and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8 million to $20 million.

Instead of acting as a sweetener it produced a furious backlash, with European football’s governing body UEFA resorting on Thursday to the nuclear option of boycotting the sport’s jewel in the crown, the World Cup.

By Saturday, Infantino held his hands up and withdrew the plan.

“Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve,” said Infantino.

August 5, 2026




 Jamaica to host historic Global Research Council Americas Regional Meeting 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica will make history this November as it hosts the Global Research Council (GRC) Americas Regional Meeting for the first time in the Caribbean.

The meeting, scheduled for November 18–19, 2026, will be hosted by the Scientific Research Council (SRC) in partnership with the United States (US) National Science Foundation (NSF) and will form part of the wider programme of the 32nd National Science and Technology Conference and Exhibition 2026, being held under the theme “Science Solves”.

In a statement on Wednesday, Executive Director of the Scientific Research Council Dr Charah Watson described the occasion as a landmark achievement for Jamaica and the Caribbean.

“Hosting the Global Research Council Americas Regional Meeting in Jamaica is both a historic milestone and a timely strategic opportunity. This comes at an important point in our own national STI journey, as the Government advances the House of Innovation as the framework for aligning research, technology, enterprise and public policy around Jamaica’s long-term development priorities,” she said.

Dr Watson continued, “The meeting gives Jamaica an opportunity to demonstrate leadership, while ensuring that the Caribbean is at the table helping to shape the research priorities, funding approaches and partnerships that will influence our future. It is essential that the perspectives of small island developing states are not peripheral to the international research agenda, but are placed front and centre as we position science, technology and innovation as key drivers of resilience, productivity and sustainable national development.”

Dr Jennifer Pearl, head of the Office of Science and Engineering at the US National Science Foundation, added, “The US National Science Foundation helped to found the Global Research Council in 2012 and is excited to partner with the Scientific Research Council of Jamaica for the upcoming meeting. Finding new approaches to curiosity-driven inquiry to accelerate scientific discovery while ensuring broader benefit to society is critical.”

The meeting will bring together heads of research councils, science funding agencies, policymakers, research and innovation leaders, development partners, and strategic stakeholders from across North America, Latin America and the Caribbean to address critical issues shaping research and innovation systems throughout the region.

A key focus of the discussions will be providing regional perspectives to inform the Global Research Council’s upcoming deliberations on curiosity-driven research, while exploring priorities including research financing, shared scientific infrastructure, resilience and natural disaster mitigation, open science, science diplomacy, improving public trust through reproducibility and transparency, evidence-informed policymaking, and opportunities for greater regional collaboration and capacity building.

August 5, 2026




 Jamaica secures 400,000 winter seats from Canada as several airline services expand 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica’s second-largest source market is poised for further growth with approximately 400,000 seats that will be available from Canada to Jamaica for the 2026/2027 winter season.

This marks a significant expansion of airlift from the Canadian market. The increase is driven by expanded service from long-standing airline partners Air Canada and Sunwing, together with new non-stop service from Porter Airlines, underscoring sustained confidence in Jamaica as a leading warm-weather destination for Canadian travellers.

The added capacity comes as Jamaica continues to strengthen its position as Canada’s preferred Caribbean destination, offering more choice, more frequency and more direct routings from key Canadian gateways into the island’s two major airports.

“This expanded airlift from Canada is a direct vote of trust and confidence in Jamaica’s tourism product and in the strength of our partnerships with Air Canada, Sunwing, WestJet and now Porter Airlines,” said Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett.

Canada remains one of Jamaica’s top-performing source markets and the additional seat capacity is expected to play a critical role in helping the destination reach its ambitious 2030 goals under the Tourism 3.0 framework, including 600,000 annual visitor arrivals from Canada and US$750 million in tourism earnings from the market.

“Reaching 600,000 annual visitors and US$750 million in earnings from Canada by 2030 requires the kind of sustained airlift growth we are seeing today,” said Donovan White, director of tourism.

The new Porter Airlines service adds a further option for Canadian travellers, joining Air Canada, Flair, Transat, Caribbean Airlines and Westjet in offering enhanced connectivity between Canada and Jamaica this winter.

“The expanded winter airlift builds on Jamaica’s broader strategy of diversifying and strengthening airlift across its top source markets, reinforcing the destination’s resilience and positioning within a competitive global tourism landscape,” said Angella Bennett, regional director of tourism for Canada at the Jamaica Tourist Board.

news.title: Trump stands by congressman accused of violence against ex-wife, toddler as deadline looms
news.text:
Donald Trump is standing by a congressman and former aide accused of multiple domestic and child abuse claims, even as other Republicans pressure him to resign.

Max Miller is refusing to quit his re-election bid after he was accused of a litany of assault claims against his ex-wife and daughter.

Miller, 37, has been accused of holding a gun to the head of his ex-wife Emily Moreno’s head.

Moreno told police that she had turned the lights on so she could change her infant daughter’s nappy in the middle of the night.

Moreno said that Miller was enraged by this, and held the gun to her head.

On another occasion, Miller allegedly threw hot water from a frying pan onto Moreno, scalding her chest and stomach.

He is also accused of breaking his daughter’s collarbone when she was two years old.

Miller has denied the accusations and accused his ex-wife of “significant mental health challenges”.

“If I had assaulted her, would she have offered to cook me dinner six days later?” Miller said.

Miller was questioned by police for seven hours but they ultimately decided not to press charges.

A former ex-girlfriend, former White House Press Secretary Stephanie Grisham, has also filed a restraining order against him.

In an effort to refute the accusations, Miller posted a Dropbox link online which contained photos that could be construed as child sexual abuse material.

The link was viewed more than 200,000 times before it was taken offline.

But Miller’s lawyer Aaron Minc said the photo was included by mistake and disputed it was abuse material.

“There were no images of ‘genitals,’” he told Politico.

“A two-year-old girl had her shirt off. That is a deliberately false, sensationalised, and disgusting characterisation.”

Miller’s former father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, is a Republican senator from Ohio.

After months of avoiding questions about the accusations against Miller, he has broken his silence.

“When he went out and did what he did — including releasing photos of my granddaughter completely naked, that now you have hundreds of thousands of psychotic human beings that have that — and to say ‘oops’ is grotesque,” Moreno said.

“My personal opinion is that this is a felony, and that every single human being that touched that photo and transmitted it electronically should go to jail because it is illegal to do that.”

Moreno described Miller as “a danger to my daughter”.

But as Moreno and other Republicans are calling for Miller to resign, he has not lost the support of Trump.

“I hope he’s able to work it out,” Trump said earlier today.

“I feel badly for him.”

Working at the White House in Trump’s first term, Miller became a favourite of the president.

When Miller and Moreno got married at one of Trump’s golf clubs in 2022, the president gave a speech.

Other Republicans meanwhile are pushing for Miller to drop out of his re-election race.

Party officials are looking anxiously at the calendar. If Miller quits before close-of-business on Monday, he can be replaced on the ballot.

If he quits after that, there will be no Republican running in his district.

Miller’s district, located in the suburbs of Cleveland, Ohio, was drawn specifically to maximise the chances of a Republican being elected.

But private polling shows Miller behind in the polls to his Democratic challenger Brian Poindexter.

“No one credibly accused of holding a gun to his wife’s head and breaking their 2-year-old daughter’s collarbone belongs in the halls of power,” Poindexter said.

The midterm elections are in November, with Democrats favoured to win the House of Representatives.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732).

news.title: Federal officials probing safety incident involving Marine One
news.text:
Aug. 5 (UPI) -- Federal aviation officials said Wednesday that they are reviewing a "loss of separation incident" between the presidential Marine One helicopter and a commercial aircraft, the latest safety incident to affect the president's air travel.

The safety incident occurred Tuesday, the National Transportation Board told UPI in an emailed statement.

President Donald Trump was aboard Marine One when it departed the Ellipse near the White House at 2:33 p.m. EDT for Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, where he boarded Air Force One en route to Los Angeles.

The NTSB said the incident occurred between Marine One and an aircraft departing Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

The Federal Aviation Administration told UPI that it was a "momentary loss of separation after which the aircraft continued to move away from one another."

"The air traffic controller was in contact with both the commercial pilot and Marine One pilot during the loss of separation," it said. "As the White House has said, the president was never in danger."

UPI has contacted the White House for comment.

The incident is the latest concern involviing the president's air travel.

Last month, Trump unexpectedly departed Turkey following a two-day NATO summit aboard an older Air Force One and then switched in Britain to the newly renovated Qatari-gifted jet on which he had arrived in Ankara.

The New York Times days later reported the jet switch was prompted by a threat that Iranian proxy militants were targeting him and his plane. Trump has denied that was the reason for the switch.

In January, an older version of Air Force One with Trump on board was forced to return to Joint Base Andrews due to an electrical issue. He had departed aboard the aircraft en route to Zurich for the World Economic Forum, but was forced to return.
news.summary: Federal aviation officials are reviewing a "loss of separation incident" between the presidential Marine One helicopter and a commercial aircraft.

news.title: 'Very difficult to communicate': Iran President Pezeshkian on Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei
news.text: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that communicating with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is "very difficult", as the latter continues to remain out of public view after succeeding his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, following his death.Pezeshkian's remarks came after US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz was likely to reopen in a day or two.Mojtaba Khamenei was also reportedly wounded in the strikes that killed the longest-serving Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Trump has repeatedly claimed that the new Supreme Leader is in "bad shape"."It is very difficult to communicate with him at the moment, but in any case, his presence is a very great source of strength for us so that we can continue," Pezeshkian said.While Mojtaba Khamenei has continued to issue written statements, his absence from public view during Iran's conflict with the United States has fuelled speculation about his ties with other senior officials.He notably did not appear at his father's funeral ceremonies last month.Pezeshkian, however, defended the Supreme Leader, saying he had held productive meetings with him and had been met with "kindness and very sound logic"."Unfortunately, the current situation allows some malicious people to describe him differently and to present a different image of him," he said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. August 5, 2026




 US refunds $100 billion in Trump tariffs 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—United States (US) President Donald Trump’s administration has refunded about $100 billion in tariffs since the Supreme Court struck down a wave of his duties this year, court filings show.

The figure, reported in documents Tuesday, constitutes about 60 percent of some $166 billion the Trump administration collected after invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose duties.

The refunds went to importers that had paid the duties.

Trump used the act to impose sweeping tariffs on trading partners since returning to the White House last year, but the high court ruled in February this year that he had exceeded his authority in doing so.

This dealt a sharp blow to the president’s ability to deploy tariffs at will, as he sought to use them as a tool for leverage against US allies and competitors alike.

The president’s sector-specific tariffs, which rely on different justifications, remain intact.

In the court filing on Tuesday, a US Customs and Border Protection official said that as of July 31, “approximately $128.68 billion in both potential and certified refunds” had been accepted for processing.

Of that total amount, refunds of around $100 billion had been completed and sent to the Treasury Department for disbursement, the official added.

Since the Supreme Court’s ruling in February, Trump has turned to new means to reimpose tariffs on dozens of partners, sparking further court challenges.

news.title: Money, money, money: Trump rakes in the cash from his social media posts
news.text:
The high-frequency traders who signed up to pay $US100,000 ($140,000) a month for early access to Donald Trump’s social media posts may already have had a demonstration of how easily they can more than recover their investments.

On Saturday, Trump Media & Technology Group’s “Truth API” went live, giving subscribers to the service access to his posts on Truth Social milliseconds before his non-paying followers saw them.

Hours after the API (application programming interface) creating a connection between the subscribers’ and Truth Social’s software was activated, Trump – who had been threatening Iran with massive air and missile strikes again, “the biggest attack since World War II” – posted that he had called off the attacks because America’s allies in the Middle East had reached the basic parameters of a deal to end the war, including a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

The oil price, not surprisingly, fell heavily. It had traded above $US90 a barrel leading into the weekend. It fell below $US84 a barrel when futures trading closed on Friday, and dropped further on Monday.
news.summary: The US president’s latest cash grab went live on the weekend, with his Trump Media & Technology’s “Truth API” giving subscribers early access to his market-moving social media posts for up to $US1.2 million a year.
news.author: Stephen Bartholomeusz

news.title: Shell shocked: Producers to give 53 million eggs to food banks in US settlement
news.text:
NEW YORK - It’s often said that you have to break a few eggs to make an omelette.

The saying rings true under a deal where three major US egg producers will have to crack into their supplies to settle price fixing claims.

Under the settlement announced on Aug 5, the companies will donate 53 million eggs to food banks.

A coalition of 17 states sued the producers, alleging they secretly coordinated to influence daily egg price quotes published by a benchmark pricing service widely used in egg supply contracts.

“It is unconscionable that these businesses colluded against hard-working New Yorkers to raise the price of eggs just to line their own pockets,” New York Attorney-General Letitia James said on Aug 5 in a statement announcing the settlement.

“The law is clear: price fixing of any kind is not tolerated in New York, or across our nation.”

James said Cal-Maine Foods, Versova and Hickman’s Egg Ranch began colluding as early as 2022.

In addition to the egg deliveries, the companies will pay US$3.3 million (S$4.23 million) to affected states and make changes to their practices to prevent future violations, the statement added.

Egg prices became a rallying point for Donald Trump in 2024‘s presidential election campaign as he sought to capitalise on voters’ frustrations with the rising cost of essential items during his predecessor Joe Biden’s presidency.

As avian flu spread like wildfire through the industry, poultry farmers were forced to cull 26 million birds, leading prices to skyrocket.

In the Big Apple, a box of 12 eggs reached an average price of US$8.47 according to a note issued by the US Department of Agriculture in February 2025.

The State of New York is to receive 4,968,000 of the eggs.

The first delivery of 280,280 was made in Brooklyn, and the others are scheduled through October.

The other states in the deal are Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Hawaii, Iowa, Maryland, Minnesota, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Utah, Vermont, and Wisconsin. AFP

news.title: Trump confronted Hegseth at Camp David over Iran munitions shortage, report says
news.text:
Donald Trump confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at Camp David last week over a munitions shortage that could limit the president’s military options in the Iran war, according to a new report.

During the exchange on the sidelines of Trump’s Cabinet meeting on Friday, Trump asked Hegseth to explain why he had apparently been misled on the dwindling weapons stockpile, saying that he thought the issue “had been fixed,” two people familiar with the matter told The Washington Post.

Hegseth had blamed his deputy, Stephen Feinberg, for the shortages and for not making sure Trump was fully informed of the issue, according to the Post’s sources. The Trump administration has denied the reporting. 

As the war drags into its sixth month, the Pentagon is reportedly running low on missile interceptors. 

The US military had 2,330 Patriot systems and 452 Terminal High Altitude Area Defense systems before the war, according to a report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies released last month. As of July 27, an estimated 759 to 827 Patriot systems and 234 to 278 THAAD systems remain, the report said. 

During a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing last month, Hegseth said US military operations in Iran have cost an estimated $37.5 billion. He also asked Congress for an additional $67 billion to, in part, replenish weapons stockpiles, blaming the Biden administration for not properly funding the Defense Department. 

“These funds will expand production lines and accelerate delivery of high-demand munitions. We're talking about solid rocket motors, JDAMs [Joint Direct Attack Munitions], hypersonics, and counter-drone capabilities,” he said during the July 21 hearing. 

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt has defended Hegseth, calling the Post’s reporting on his Camp David exchange with Trump “100% fake news.”

“Literally never happened. And President Trump has the utmost confidence in Secretary Hegseth,” Leavitt told the publication. 

Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell also denied the reporting, telling the Post, “Secretary Hegseth did not mislead anyone about our munitions posture, and he did not blame Deputy Secretary Feinberg. These claims about depleted stockpiles, internal disagreements…are equally fictional.”

The Independent has reached out to the White House, which referred to Leavitt’s statement, and the Defense Department for comment.

Despite the report about Trump grilling Hegseth in private, Hegseth was publicly praising the president during Friday’s Cabinet meeting. 

Hegseth talked about Trump having the “courage to undertake Epic Fury and this Iranian regime and ensure they never have a nuclear weapon…and, frankly, the courage to negotiate with people that have shown no willingness to do so honestly.”
news.summary: The Pentagon chief reportedly blamed his deputy, Stephen Feinberg, for not making sure the president was fully informed of the issue
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Brewery Offering Drink Deals When Trump, McConnell Die Keeps License
news.text: A Wisconsin brewery known for its controversial drink promotions tied to the deaths of President Donald Trump and Senator Mitch McConnell remains open as the owner fights a pending alcohol permit revocation. Minocqua Brewing Company was set to have its license revoked on Tuesday, after state officials moved against the business, citing alleged violations of Wisconsin alcohol regulations. However, the brewery has since launched an appeal challenging the notice of permit revocation, which allows it to remain open for business during the legal process, according to the Wisconsin Division of Alcohol Beverage. "Today was the day that Wisconsin's Department of Revenue was supposed to shut us down," the brewery wrote in a post announcing that it remained open. "Guess what? We're still alive and Kickin'!" Owner Kirk Bangstad has argued that the state's action against the brewery was politically motivated, calling it “an absurd act of heavy-handedness" following the company's announcements of promotions offering free beer after Trump's death and half-price beer after McConnell's death. Bangstad also vowed to “fight tooth and nail” to keep the brewery operating, adding, "they’ll have to pry me out of my taprooms before I stop selling beer to thirsty progressives who come to visit us.” The Wisconsin Department of Revenue confirmed it has "issued notice of a Brewer’s permit revocation for two Minocqua Brewing Company locations and notice of an Alcohol Beverage Warehouse permit revocation for one location." The move came after officials seized canned beer from the brewery in June over allegations it had been illegally transported from Illinois without securing the proper permits or paying the appropriate taxes, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. "The Wisconsin Division of Alcohol Beverages is dedicated to the fair and consistent enforcement of alcohol beverages regulations in Wisconsin," the department said. "'The division is required to follow and implement state law, including ensuring permit holders and licensees follow all applicable laws and regulations. The division takes appropriate actions when these laws are not followed.” Bangstad declined to provide further comment when reached by Newsweek. Backlash Over the Controversial Promos Minocqua Brewing Company said it received a wave of hostile messages and negative reactions after announcing #freebeerday, a promotion offering free beer on the day Trump dies. Bangstad claimed supporters of Trump flooded the brewery’s social media pages and phone lines with criticism following the announcement. The brewery has also faced backlash over #halfpricebeerday, a separate promotion tied to the death of McConnell. Critics have questioned whether businesses should celebrate the deaths of political opponents, while supporters of the brewery have defended the promotions as protected political speech. Bangstad has continued defending the campaigns, arguing that the controversy has increased attention for the brewery and boosted sales of beer and merchandise. Where Is Mitch McConnell Now? McConnell remains in office but has been largely out of public view following a June hospitalization after a fall. The 84-year-old Kentucky Republican has not returned to the Senate, and his extended absence has fueled questions about his health and whether he is able to continue carrying out his duties. McConnell's office initially provided few details about his condition, saying only that he was recovering and continuing to work with staff. The lack of public appearances led to growing scrutiny from lawmakers, political observers and critics who questioned why there had not been a more detailed update on his health. After weeks of limited information, McConnell's office released a statement explaining that he had fallen, was briefly unconscious and had been hospitalized. They said doctors determined he did not suffer a heart attack, stroke, broken bones or a concussion, but that he developed a mild case of pneumonia while receiving treatment. His office later said McConnell was undergoing rehabilitation and physical therapy and had not yet been medically cleared to resume Senate duties. Officials said his recovery has been affected by mobility issues related to a childhood case of polio. Mitch McConnell Status: Latest Updates McConnell has not announced plans to resign and has said he intends to complete his current Senate term, which ends in January. His office has said he remains engaged with staff on Senate and Kentucky matters while he recovers. The prolonged absence has drawn political attention in Kentucky, particularly because of questions over what would happen if McConnell left office before the end of his term. Kentucky Democratic Governor Andy Beshear has called for greater transparency on McConnell's condition, while the senator's office has maintained that he is recovering and plans to return to his duties. The lack of regular public appearances has also contributed to speculation online, but McConnell's office and medical officials have said his absence is related to recovery from his fall, pneumonia and mobility challenges rather than a decision to step away from office. Brewery's License Fight Continues Bangstad said his attorney contacted the state Department of Revenue regarding the appeal process and that the brewery expects the dispute could take months to resolve. The brewery has also claimed that increased attention surrounding the controversy has boosted sales of beer and merchandise. The Department of Revenue said in an earlier statement that the brewery had until Tuesday to appeal and "can operate during the appeal process." "Should the business decide to appeal, the next step would be to appeal to the Secretary of the Department of Revenue, who will assign the appeal to a Department of Revenue hearing examiner for their recommendations as to proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law.” Newsweek has reached out to the Wisconsin Department of Revenue for further comment. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: A Wisconsin brewery known for its controversial drink promotions remains open as the owner fights a pending permit revocation.
news.author: Hannah Parry

news.title: Yen and dollar drift on Iran deal concerns, payroll jitters
news.text:
HONG KONG, Aug 6 : Currency markets drifted on Thursday with the yen struggling to retain intervention gains and the dollar pinned near six-week lows, as concerns about a proposed U.S.-Iran deal and jitters about upcoming U.S. payroll data left traders cautious. 

The yen was little changed at 157.71 per dollar in early trade after weakening for two straight sessions. It has now given back some intervention gains after touching 155.20 per dollar on Monday, but remains well off last month's multi-decade low of about 164.

The euro was little changed at $1.1557, and sterling traded flat at $1.3469. The New Zealand dollar and the Australian dollar were also flat, last trading at $0.5885 and $0.7056, respectively.

The dollar index, which tracks the U.S. currency against six major peers, was little changed at 99.65, struggling to find direction while hovering near a six-week low.

Markets remained watchful as tensions continued to play out in the Gulf after Reuters reported a proposed deal between Iran and Oman to help end the U.S.-Iran conflict could give Tehran control over inbound traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

There was no immediate U.S. comment on the proposal. President Donald Trump has said a deal to reopen the strait was imminent, but U.S. officials have repeatedly insisted they would never agree to Iran controlling access to the world's most important trade route for energy supplies.

Brent crude futures fell 0.5 per cent to $79.08 a barrel on Thursday, near the levels last seen when the U.S. and Iran signed an interim peace agreement in June. 

"The market's very much in sort of watch and wait mode," Ray Attrill, head of FX strategy at National Australia Bank, said in a podcast. 

"We haven't got the oil market volatility that has really been the key driver of most markets in recent days and weeks," he said, adding that markets were waiting to see whether a deal would be struck at all. 

CENTRAL BANKS IN FOCUS 

Bank of Japan policymakers debated mounting price risks that likely required more rate hikes even as they raised borrowing costs to a 31-year high in June, minutes of the meeting showed on Wednesday. 

That highlights growing attention within the board to broadening price pressures, further bolstering the case for another rate hike as soon as September.

Fuelled by interventions from Tokyo and coordinated action with Washington in recent days, the yen rallied as much as 5 per cent against the dollar but was struggling to retain the gains.

In a recent Reuters poll, nearly 95 per cent of the respondents said future Japanese currency interventions alone would not sustainably curb the currency's weakness. Nearly every respondent who said that also said the BOJ would have to raise interest rates to make a lasting impact.

Investors are now also awaiting U.S. payroll data that could provide more clues on the Federal Reserve's interest rate path, after data showed the country's services sector stayed strong in July even as input costs rose, but services-sector employment slowed. 

A Reuters survey of economists expected July's employment report on Friday to show nonfarm payrolls increased by 80,000 jobs in July after rising 57,000 in June. The unemployment rate is forecast to hold steady at 4.2 per cent. 

Fed Governor Lisa Cook said on Wednesday that she was open to the idea that the central bank may need to raise its short-term interest rate target to deal with "too high" levels of inflation in the U.S. economy.

news.title: 'Safety incident' involving Trump's helicopter as White House releases statement
news.text: Transport officials are looking into why passenger jet was allowed to take off as Marine Forces One approached with the US president on board. US President Donald Trump's helicopter as approaching Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Tuesday, August 4 when the incident occurred in what could be a violation of safety procedures . The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said on Wednesday they were investigating what happened. Poor communication between the military and the civilian air traffic controllers at Reagan has been an issue in the past. Last year, 67 people lost their lives when an airliner collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter. As a result, the FAA decided that all take-offs and landings at the Washington, DC airport would be halted anytime a helicopter passes by on a conflicting route. The airspace near the White House and Reagan is heavily congested with military and commercial aircraft. The two aircraft were not on a collision course as the passenger jet was climbing above Marine One as the helicopter approached. The FAA said in a statement that "there was a momentary loss of separation after which the aircraft continued to move away from one another." "The air traffic controller was in contact with both the commercial pilot and Marine One pilot during the loss of separation," the FAA said. The White House said that Trump was never in danger. "Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm’s way," White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement. The Marine Corps defended the actions of their helicopter pilots.
news.author: Tannur Anders

news.title: Hiroshima mayor criticizes Russia, makes no mention of US in bombing anniversary speech
news.text:
TOKYO, August 6. /TASS/. Hiroshima Mayor Kazumi Matsui criticized Russia and its actions in Ukraine during a memorial ceremony marking the 81st anniversary of the US atomic bombing but did not name the United States as the country that dropped the bomb on the city.

Matsui began his speech by accusing Russia of allegedly "using nuclear weapons as a tool of intimidation" and criticizing its actions in Ukraine. At first, he did not name Russia, referring to it as a "major power," but later directly mentioned the country and the conflict in Ukraine.

At the same time, as in previous years, the Hiroshima mayor never said that the United States had carried out the 1945 atomic bombing. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also made no mention of the US in her address. She pledged that Japan would continue doing everything possible to advance nuclear disarmament and create a world without nuclear weapons. "We must not stop moving along this path," she stressed. Matsui likewise called for nuclear disarmament and expressed hope that the world would never see a third city suffer an atomic bombing.

Japanese officials generally do not emphasize in public speeches that the United States carried out the attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. In previous years, Japanese prime ministers and the mayors of both cities also refrained from directly naming the US in their remarks at ceremonies commemorating the tragedy. However, the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum presents comprehensive information about the atomic bombings of 1945. Japanese school and university textbooks cover their history in detail as well.

The United States carried out the atomic bombings of the two cities at the very end of World War II, with the officially stated aim of accelerating Japan’s surrender. They remain the only instances of nuclear weapons being used in warfare in human history. According to various estimates, the bomb dropped on Hiroshima killed between 70,000 and 100,000 people on the day of the explosion. By the end of 1945, the death toll had risen to 140,000 as people died in hospitals from their injuries and radiation exposure. The total number of victims of the bombing now exceeds 350,000.

The United States still does not acknowledge moral responsibility for the atomic bombings, justifying its actions as a "military necessity." Former President Joe Biden, who attended the Group of Seven summit in Hiroshima in May 2023, did not apologize for the nuclear attacks. Neither did Barack Obama, who in 2016 became the first sitting US president to visit the memorial. US President Donald Trump has not visited the memorials in Hiroshima or Nagasaki, although the two Japanese cities invited him both during his first presidential term and after his return to the White House.
news.summary: Kazumi Matsui began his speech by accusing Russia of allegedly "using nuclear weapons as a tool of intimidation"
news.author: Tass

news.title: Why was a plane allowed to take off as Trump's helicopter approached
news.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is investigating why a commercial aircraft was cleared for take-off from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while US President Donald Trump's helicopter, Marine One, was approaching the airport, despite safety procedures introduced after last year's deadly midair collision.The incident took place on Tuesday as Marine One carried Trump from the White House to Andrews Air Force Base for the first leg of his West Coast trip. Although officials said the aircraft were never on a collision course and the president was never in danger, the event has raised fresh questions about whether the stricter safety measures introduced after January 2025's fatal crash are being properly followed.Both the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are gathering information about the incident. While the FAA has launched a preliminary investigation, the NTSB said it was still assessing the circumstances before deciding whether to open a separate probe. What happened over Reagan National Airport?According to the FAA, the commercial jet took off as Marine One was approaching Reagan National Airport. The plane climbed above the presidential helicopter, meaning the two aircraft were moving apart rather than towards one another.Even so, the FAA said there was a "momentary loss of separation" between the aircraft. Air traffic controllers remained in contact with both the airline crew and the Marine One pilots throughout the incident.The agency has not explained why the commercial flight was authorised to depart while Marine One was inbound. The Wall Street Journal first reported the incident.The White House sought to reassure the public, saying Trump was never at risk. "Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm's way," White House spokesperson Kush Desai said.The US Marine Corps also rejected suggestions of a near miss. Spokesperson Capt. Jacob Sugg said there were no "close calls" and that controllers neither delayed nor altered the helicopter's flight path, instead providing appropriate traffic information throughout the journey. Why is the incident drawing scrutiny?The investigation comes just months after a catastrophic collision on 29 January 2025, when a passenger airliner and a US Army Black Hawk helicopter crashed near Reagan National Airport, killing all 67 people aboard the two aircraft.Following that disaster, the FAA introduced stricter operating procedures for the airport's notoriously congested airspace. The rules require all take-offs and landings to be suspended whenever helicopters travel along conflicting routes near the airport. Controllers are also required to use radar rather than visual separation, while military aircraft must continuously broadcast their locations.The latest incident has prompted renewed criticism from families of those killed in last year's crash, who questioned whether enough has been been done to improve safety around Reagan National. The group has continued to urge Congress to adopt aviation safety reforms recommended by the NTSB.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

news.title: Judge criticizes the Justice Department as he dismisses Jan. 6 seditious conspiracy case
news.text: WASHINGTON — A federal judge decried efforts to rewrite the history of the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as he reluctantly dismissed the seditious conspiracy case against members of the far-right Oath Keepers extremist group at the Trump administration’s request. The move Tuesday closes the book on the Jan. 6 cases that were wiped out with Republican President Donald Trump’s sweeping pardons and commutations last year, freeing people convicted of violent assaults on police and other crimes from prison. The Department of Justice in April acted to vacate the convictions of Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes and others in the seditious conspiracy case, who had their sentences commuted but did not receive pardons. It was a stunning reversal from the Democratic Biden administration, which hailed the guilty verdicts in one of the most serious cases stemming from the Capitol attack. U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta, who oversaw the Oath Keepers’ trials, criticized the department’s move, writing in his ruling that the government “asks to absolve these Defendants of crimes against the United States itself.” But Mehta wrote that he had no choice but to grant the administration’s request. “This is the last of the prosecutions seeking to hold accountable those responsible for the events of Jan. 6. That book is now closed,” wrote Mehta, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama. “Today’s epilogue diminishes the gravity of that day, denigrates the work of the prosecutors and law enforcement officers who secured these convictions, and excuses criminal acts that caused a centuries-long pillar of our democracy — the peaceful transfer of presidential power — to buckle. The court cannot write a different ending,” he wrote. US President Donald Trump’s military helicopter Marine One briefly flew too close to a passenger jet taking off from Washington’s Reagan National airport, prompting investigations by both the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board.

The FAA said in a statement that its preliminary safety review of the incident on Tuesday found “a momentary loss of separation, after which the aircraft continued to move away from one another”.

The statement added that Trump was not in danger and that an air traffic controller remained in contact with both pilots throughout.

According to the Reuters news agency, two people familiar with the matter said that air traffic controllers had not paused commercial departures at Reagan National as required under the policy adopted after a crash last year.

In January 2025, a collision between a military helicopter and an American Airlines regional jet killed 67 people.

Marine One lifted off from the Ellipse near the White House at about 2:33pm local time (18:33 GMT) on Tuesday, en route to Joint Base Andrews ahead of a presidential trip to Los Angeles, according to a White House pool report.

Both the aircraft landed safely, although neither flight’s involvement has been confirmed by the FAA.

A source told Reuters that Envoy Air flight 3742, a regional jet operated on behalf of American Airlines and bound for Pensacola, Florida, was the aircraft involved, and that a second flight, Republic 4700, was separately rerouted as a precaution after coming within three miles of the airport.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it would launch its own investigation into the incident.

The near-miss on Tuesday afternoon revives scrutiny of air traffic protocols at Reagan National following the collision last year.

The crash then led to permanent restrictions on mixed helicopter and commercial traffic at the airport, along with a subsequent ban, introduced in March, on using visual-only separation for helicopters near major US airports.

news.title: Iran says agreement on Strait of Hormuz at ‘final stage’
news.text:
Iran said on Wednesday it is in the “final stage” of drafting an agreement with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz, following US President Donald Trump saying a deal could be announced this week.

The deal could reopen the critical waterway, but the agreement is likely to be contingent on the US lifting its blockade on Iran’s ports.

The Trump administration has previously ruled out any deal that would cement Iran’s grip over the strait.

Iran has insisted on some measure of control over the strait, saying it will not go back to being an open international waterway, as it was before the war.

Closure of the strait, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and natural gas once passed, has driven up the price of fuel and basic goods, roiling the global economy.

Mr Trump is also under mounting pressure to end an unpopular war ahead of US congressional elections.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the agreement with Oman is in the “final stage” of drafting and that a joint statement will be issued “if certain parties do not obstruct this process,” apparently referring to the US

The draft deal to reopen the strait was awaiting final approval from Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, two regional officials told The Associated Press on Wednesday.

Mr Khamenei is believed to have been wounded in the war’s opening strikes and has not been seen in public since then.

The officials portrayed the potential deal as a temporary solution to the dispute over the strait. They said it is tied to an agreement reached between the US and Iran in June, which aimed at ending the fighting and reopening the waterway but ultimately collapsed.

They said the potential deal will pave the way for the US and Iran to resume negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear programme.

Earlier, they said the potential agreement would have ships enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through a route controlled by Oman. Service fees would be charged for providing security and preserving the maritime environment.

The US has said it is strongly opposed to any arrangement that would see Iran charge fees.

Mr Trump was asked on Tuesday evening by reporters about a report that an announcement on the strait could be made on Wednesday.

“It could happen. Tomorrow or the next day,” Mr Trump said. “A lot of progress has been made.”

Vice President JD Vance acknowledged on Wednesday that it can seem like the US is not making progress in Iran, describing the effort to end the war as “messy” and that “it’s going to take some time”.

Mr Vance told Fox News the Iranians are “extraordinarily difficult people” and that efforts to try to resolve the war sometimes require moving backward before moving forward.

The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed on Wednesday they had fired ballistic missiles towards a Saudi oil tanker on the Red Sea off the Saudi port of Yanbu, without providing evidence. There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.

A vessel sailing in the Gulf of Aden off Yemen reported a loud explosion that happened in close proximity, the British military’s United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said on Wednesday, adding that the crew was safe.

The Houthis claimed to have fired a ballistic missile at another Saudi oil tanker.

news.title: Tucker Carlson Lays Out 10 Ways to 'Rebuild' America As MAGA Split Widens
news.text: Former Fox News host Tucker Carlson on Wednesday laid out 10 qualities he feels America should always possess, as "Our political system has collapsed into paralysis and looting." His remarks on The Tucker Carlson Show seemingly escalate his break with President Donald Trump, exposing tensions within the coalition that helped return Trump to the White House. "It's been obvious for a while now that our system is not working as intended, because the people in charge of it seem to be looking out mostly, not exclusively, but mostly for their own interests," Carlson said. "So, it's one thing to have a system run by people who are looking out for their own best interest, and not yours, again, we've had that. It's another to have a system that's totally incapable of responding to reality. It is basically paralyzed," he later added, saying that the latter is the one plaguing America today. Carlson touched on what he labeled the two biggest threats in all of history, nuclear war and artificial intelligence, saying they are looming right in front of us all, and that those with authority are "frozen." He listed in extensive detail 10 traits America should have, while saying "change is coming." The virtues included a recommitment to fairness, sovereignty, being productive, having beauty, health, honesty, being optimistic, wise, showing decency and being united. Carlson also touched on immigration and having Americans speak English. "Different languages divide," he said. "If you were serious about holding your country together ... you'd be serious above all about making certain that everyone in your country spoke the same language." "Both parties have colluded against the population to make their lives better and our lives worse," he also said. In concluding his nearly two-hour segment, Carlson said, "So if you're going to fix it and rebuild this country and turn it into a place that the grandchildren you hopefully will have can inherit and thrive, you're going to need to do something about the pressing question of American identity. 'What does it mean to be an American?' But it's fixable, you just have to try, and we will be trying. And we'll tell you, as we continue to do that." The move comes 90 days before the November 3 midterm elections, with control of the House and Senate at stake. Carlson first signaled his plans to help build a third party in a July 1 interview with the Columbia Journalism Review, saying the country was operating as a "one-party state disguised as a democracy" and arguing that the political system needed to be disrupted. "I'm going to help build a third party," Carlson said in the interview, adding that he did not intend to run for office himself. The split between Carlson and parts of the MAGA coalition reflects a broader tension within Trump's movement. Trump built much of his political identity around challenging Washington's foreign policy establishment and reducing U.S. involvement abroad, but decisions during his presidency, including the war with Iran, have frustrated supporters who favor a more strictly non-interventionist approach. Carlson's influence within the Republican base remains difficult to measure. A 2025 Pew Research Center study found that 9 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents said they often got news from the Tucker Carlson Network. Trump, meanwhile, has maintained strong approval ratings among self-identified Republicans despite the feud, though the Iran war has weakened his standing with the broader coalition. Tucker Carlson Leads MAGA Break With Trump The new video somewhat hardens a break that has been building inside the president's coalition since the United States entered the war with Iran. Former U.S. Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene, a Republican, posted a photograph on August 1 showing herself seated at a table at Carlson's studio in Maine. Also in the image were her husband, conservative journalist Brian Glenn; U.S. Representative Thomas Massie, also a Republican, and his wife, Carolyn Moffa; and Joe Kent, former director of the National Counterterrorism Center, and his wife, Heather Kent. "We said no more foreign wars and we meant it," Greene, of Georgia, wrote alongside the photograph. She said Trump had betrayed his supporters and described the group's commitment as America First for Americans across the political spectrum. She closed the post by declaring that the movement had begun. The group did not announce a party name, an organizational structure or any legal filings at the time. Greene's post used the word movement rather than party. Each figure in the photograph has been sidelined by Trump in recent months. Greene left Congress this year after the president withdrew his endorsement. Massie lost his Republican primary in May to Ed Gallrein, a retired Navy SEAL whom Trump recruited and backed. Kent resigned as director of the National Counterterrorism Center in March in protest of the war with Iran. In a June 22 post on X, Greene said she was done with the Republican Party and suggested many others felt the same way, while making clear that her break did not mean she was becoming a Democrat. Carlson, who has long opposed American military involvement in the Middle East, struck a similar tone in a June 18 interview on the Can't Be Censored podcast, saying he had no plans to support either major party. At the time, he said he was unsure what he would do next. The structural barriers to a third-party challenge remain significant. Winner-take-all elections, the Electoral College and state ballot access rules have historically made it difficult for outside movements to translate national dissatisfaction into electoral victories. Ross Perot won roughly 19 percent of the popular vote in 1992 but no electoral votes. The America Party floated by Elon Musk in 2025 was never formally established. Public frustration with the two-party system is widespread but has yet to translate into a viable alternative. Gallup's annual governance survey, conducted September 2 to 16, found that 62 percent of American adults said a third party was needed because the two major parties were doing such a poor job. That was nearly identical to the record high of 63 percent recorded in 2023, while 30 percent said the two parties were doing an adequate job. Timeline of the MAGA-Trump fallout Donald Trump’s Approval Rating Among Republican Pollsters The latest poll from McLaughlin & Associates, affiliated with Trump, showed that 36 percent of Americans approve of both Trump and his policies, while 13 percent said they approved of only his policies. In that poll, 47 percent of respondents said they did not approve of Trump. That marks a slight shift from August 2025, when 38 percent of respondents said they approved of Trump and his policies and 14 percent approved of just his policies; 45 percent said they disapproved of Trump at the time. McLaughlin & Associates' latest poll surveyed 1,000 general election voters from July 15-21. Rasmussen Reports, another pollster viewed as being more Republican, showed Trump underwater. In its daily tracking poll for Monday, 44 percent of likely U.S. voters said they approved of Trump’s job performance, compared to 55 percent who disapproved. Twenty-five percent said they strongly approved of his job performance, while 46 percent strongly disapproved, according to the poll. It was conducted among 1,500 likely voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A recent Cygnal poll did not track Trump’s approval in terms of job performance but instead his personal favorability. It found that 56.1 percent of Americans viewed Trump favorably, compared to 41.9 percent who viewed him unfavorably. It surveyed 1,500 respondents on June 30 and July 1 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.53 percentage points. A poll from J.L. Partners and The Daily Mail showed that 56 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump, compared to 44 percent who approved of him. It surveyed 1,000 registered voters from July 17-20. How Does That Compare to Independent Polls? Several major pollsters released surveys last month showing that Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low, raising red flags about his standing among independent voters and even parts of his base. A Quinnipiac University poll showed Trump’s approval at 32 percent—its lowest point from either of his terms. It surveyed 963 registered voters from July 23-27. A CNN poll also found a record low in Trump approval at 34 percent. It surveyed 1,225 respondents, also from July 23-27. An AP-NORC poll, which surveyed 1,165 adults on the same days, showed his approval at 33 percent, tied with April for the lowest ever. news.title: OpenAI forced to pay $3.2 million for shutting out US workers
news.text:
OpenAI has agreed to pay $3.2 million to settle US government claims that it discriminated against American job applicants while favoring foreign workers with temporary visas.

The US Justice Department said on Tuesday that the tech giant and its subsidiary Statsig, which makes product development software, deliberately made some vacancies harder for American workers to find and apply for.

OpenAI allegedly failed to post the positions on its public careers website, required applicants to mail paper applications instead of applying electronically, and advertised some jobs on the radio late at night.

Officials said the measures discouraged Americans from applying, making it easier for the companies to claim that they could not find suitable domestic workers and justify hiring foreign visa holders instead.

“It is illegal to discriminate against US workers by preferring temporary visa holders for jobs,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon said.

Under the settlement, OpenAI will pay $1.2 million in penalties and establish a $2 million fund to compensate people allegedly harmed by the recruitment practices. The company must also revise its hiring policies, publicly advertise relevant vacancies, accept electronic applications, train recruitment staff and submit to Justice Department monitoring.

Although fewer than ten positions were involved, officials said the size of the settlement reflected the harm caused when American applicants are shut out of lucrative technology jobs.

OpenAI has denied any wrongdoing.

The case comes amid US President Donald Trump’s wider campaign against alleged abuse of foreign-worker visa programs. He has argued that major companies use such schemes to hire cheaper labor from abroad at the expense of American employees.

Last year, Trump imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications, saying the surcharge would protect US jobs and national security. A federal judge blocked the measure in June, ruling that the White House could not impose what amounted to a tax without congressional approval.

Supporters of skilled-worker visas have argued that they allow US companies to fill specialized positions and help the country remain competitive in technology and other advanced industries. Trump’s critics have also opposed his restrictions on the H-1B program, arguing they would harm schools, universities, hospitals and other public institutions that rely on foreigners.

OpenAI has agreed to pay $3.2 million to settle claims that it discriminated against US workers while favoring foreign applicants

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Endures Scores Of Islamophobic Attacks After Michigan Primary Win
news.text:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, faced a slew of bigoted attacks following his primary win on Tuesday. 

While President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance had their own vitriol for the progressive Democrat, other right-wing figures and lawmakers opted to attack El-Sayed’s ethnicity and Muslim faith. 

Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the Republican nominee for Senate in Michigan, claimed El-Sayed said the U.S. deserved the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. 

“I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice. Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11,” Rogers said in his statement.

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) followed Rogers’ lead.

“Can we stop electing terrorists into office in America?” Mace said in a social media post on Wednesday. 

Laura Loomer, a self-proclaimed “proud Islamophobe” and close ally of Trump, posted a series of attacks against El-Sayed along with unfounded conspiracy theories about Muslim-Americans. 

“The official Democrat Party account just openly endorsed an Islamic jihadist who signed a pledge in support of the Muslim Brotherhood, a designated foreign Islamic terrorist organization. Abdul El Sayed mourned the death of the Ayatollah. Democrats support Islamic terrorism,” Loomer wrote in one post. 

“Mosques all across America are being used to stockpile military-grade rifles, grenades, knives and explosives to arm millions of military-aged Muslim men and illegal alien invaders,” she wrote in another. 

The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) quickly posted an attack ad against El-Sayed that was full of Islamophobic dog whistles, repeating the 9/11 claims and allegeding he supports the leader of the Muslim Brotherhood. 

“El-Sayed is the most radical Democrat Senate nominee ever. His support of terrorist organizations, socialist policies, and the defunding of law enforcement makes him dangerous and ultimately disqualified from serving,” Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), the chair of the NRSC, said in a statement posted with the attack ad.

My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries,” El-Sayed said.

news.title: Pacific islands alarmed by Trump-backed push for deep-sea mining
news.text: A Pacific island leader says there were "no consultations" before the US announced swathes of nearby ocean could be auctioned for deep-sea mining exploration, telling AFP the industry faced strong opposition among his people. Commonwealth of Northern Mariana Islands Governor David Apatang said the idea had caused great unease across the tropical island chain of some 40,000 people. The United States alarmed its tropical island territories earlier this year, detailing plans to carve up parts of the Pacific Ocean for mining exploration. Mining companies see enormous wealth in mineral deposits scattered across the seabed, but the fledgling industry has for years been held back by environmental concerns. An expanse of US maritime territory near American Samoa in the South Pacific could be auctioned as soon as November, according to official documents. Separate tracts of ocean surrounding Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific are also under consideration. "Some concerns include disruption to food security for the people of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, who rely on the ocean resources for their survival," Apatang told AFP. Washington initially proposed to explore a 140,000 square kilometre (50,000 square mile) block about 200 kilometres east of territory capital Saipan. But Apatang said he was caught by surprise when the US announced in March that a similar-sized block to Saipan's west could be leased as well. "There have been no consultations with the people of the Northern Mariana Islands," he said. The US is considering deep-sea mining exploration in two blocks east and west of Saipan, the capital of the Northern Mariana Islands. (768x511, AR: 1.50)Deep-sea mining companies want to scour the ocean's abyssal plains for mineral deposits and polymetallic nodules laden with nickel, copper and cobalt. - 'Unleashing' resources - US President Donald Trump signed an executive order in 2025 aimed at "unleashing" these seabed resources, stressing the demand in everything from renewable energy to military applications. Critics fear deep-sea mining will cause irreversible damage, smothering marine life in plumes of waste and disrupting oceanic migrations with the thrum of heavy machinery. The Mariana Islands, Guam and American Samoa all want at least a temporary ban on deep-sea mining in their territorial waters. But the US territories -- which rely on Washington for funding and defence -- have little say on what Washington does outside their three mile (five kilometre) maritime boundary. Guam passed laws this year banning deep-sea mining vessels from calling at its ports, potentially hampering the industry by cutting off a crucial source of fuel and supplies. Apatang said the Northern Mariana Islands would "consider following suit". Plans for deep-sea mining exploration are most advanced for a vast sweep of ocean near American Samoa, a US territory nestled between New Zealand and Hawaii in the South Pacific. The US Bureau of Ocean Energy Management is proposing to hold an auction in November, selling exploration licenses for a 125,000 square kilometre block. The area borders the vast Rose Atoll marine sanctuary, where endangered species of Hawksbill turtle thrive on vibrant reefs. Many in the US territory of American Samoa are staunchly opposed to deep-sea mining in the waters near their archipelago. (768x511, AR: 1.50)Lawmaker Aumua Amata, who represents American Samoa in the US House of Representatives, said she worried deep-sea mining could disrupt fisheries providing the vast bulk of the territory's export earnings. "I represent our people and I am confident that a majority of American Samoans are opposed," she told AFP. The licenses cover preliminary surveys and sampling, with future decisions on commercial exploitation needing further bureau approval. - Money for 'nothing' - American Samoa-based environmental advocate Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka said it was impossible to put a "price tag" on the ocean. "It's not something you think: 'How much money can you make off it?'." Former US diplomat Emily Wood has been working with the Guam governor's office to better understand the risks of deep-sea mining. She said leading mining company Impossible Metals had pledged to share one percent of profits with island communities. "That's nothing at all, compared to the potential damage they might cause," she told AFP. Impossible Metals did not reply to a request for comment. The company has previously stated it will not start mining until it is satisfied it is safe. Pacific island nations are divided on whether deep-sea mining will deliver economic windfalls, or environmental catastrophe. Nauru and the Cook Islands are among world leaders in seabed mining exploration, while the likes of Samoa, Fiji and Palau have called for a moratorium on the industry. The US Bureau of Ocean Energy Management was approached for comment. sft/oho/fox/lga

news.title: Investigators look at why a plane was allowed to take off as President Trump’s helicopter approached
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — It’s not clear why a plane was allowed to take off as President Donald Trump’s helicopter was approaching Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Tuesday afternoon in an apparent violation of safety procedures put in place after last year’s midair collision near the busy airport.

Both the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said Wednesday they were investigating what happened when a commercial jet took off just as Marine One left the White House for Andrews Air Force Base with the president aboard for the first leg of a West Coast trip.

The FAA decided after 67 people died on Jan. 29, 2025, when an airliner collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter that all takeoffs and landings at the Washington, D.C., airport would be halted anytime a helicopter passes by on a conflicting route. The airspace near the White House and Reagan is heavily congested with military and commercial aircraft.

The airplane that took off Tuesday was climbing above Marine One as the helicopter approached, so the two aircraft were not on a collision course.

The FAA said in a statement that a preliminary investigation showed “there was a momentary loss of separation after which the aircraft continued to move away from one another.”

“The air traffic controller was in contact with both the commercial pilot and Marine One pilot during the loss of separation,” the FAA said.

The White House emphasized that Trump was never in danger.

“Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm’s way,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement.

The Marine Corps defended the actions of their helicopter pilots.

“There were no ‘close calls’ with the routine Marine One movement,” Marine Corps spokesperson Capt. Jacob Sugg said in an email. “Washington National Tower did not delay the helicopter crew, ask them to hold, or otherwise alter their flight profile.”

The Wall Street Journal first reported the incident.

Poor communication between the military and the civilian air traffic controllers at Reagan has been an issue in the past. It came out last spring after one of the hearings on the midair collision that a hotline connecting the Pentagon to the tower at Reagan hadn’t been working for more than three years, and the FAA hadn’t even realized it.

The FAA took steps to ensure that helicopters and airplanes would no longer share the same airspace around the airport shortly after the investigation into last year’s collision began. The rules also require air traffic controllers to use radar — and not rely on pilots’ eyes — to maintain separation and require all military aircraft to broadcast their locations.

The main group of family members of the victims of last year’s crash questioned why the government hasn’t done more to prevent collisions in the crowded airspace around Reagan in a post Wednesday on the social platform X. The family members have been urging Congress to reach a compromise and pass the package of aviation safety reforms that the NTSB recommended after the midair collision.
